questions.q: In the first poem, the poet addresses Latika with the phrase "पकड़ पियु ;स लंसलक्स य्स लतिका द्स" (Pakad piyu ;s lansalaks ys latika ds). What is the literal meaning of this address, and what does it immediately establish about the relationship between speaker and addressee?
questions.a: The phrase means "Hold [my] hand, this is for Latika" or "Catch hold, beloved, these verses are for Latika." It establishes that the poems are explicitly dedicated to her, positioning her as the sole audience and purpose of the poetic act. A wrong answer (e.g., "The poet is asking Latika to hold his hand physically") reveals a literalist reading that misses the metaphorical dedication and the literary convention of offering verses to a patron/muse.

questions.q: The first poem uses the line "द्ग द्ग व्कौ न्छ्य्स एउह्कौ द्स" (dag dag vkau Nchys euHkkou ds) and "क्स्ग क्स्ग ज्क्क्फ्र घ न्सा न्सा लुएकु द्स" (xfg xfg jk[kfr gh nSa nSa lueku ds). Explain in your own words what these paired images (burning/cooling, watching/weighing) suggest about the *effect* Latika has on the speaker, and therefore about her implied character.
questions.a: The paired contrasts (burning vs. cooling the heart; watching vs. weighing the body) suggest Latika simultaneously inflames passion and brings peace, and that the speaker's very existence is measured by her gaze. This portrays her as a powerful, almost divine force who controls the speaker's inner state. A wrong answer that lists the images without synthesizing their combined effect (e.g., "It shows she is hot and cold") misses the *integration* of opposites that defines her characterization as a complete, governing presence.

questions.q: In the second poem, the poet asks: "वुक्द्कुह व्क्ज्ल्ह फुग्क्फ्ज्क्स द्ज्क्स्यस द्स्य्क्स?" (vukdkuh vkjlh fugkfjcks djkSxs dkSyks?) and later says "ओव्क्द ह्क्ज्ह एव्द्र्क च्य्क; व्कि च्क्स्फ्य्ग्स" (owQdHkjh ewdrk cqyk; vki cksfy gS). Apply the concept of *rhetorical question* and *hyperbole* to explain how these lines construct Latika's character as someone whose *silence* and *anger* are both unbearable.
questions.a: The rhetorical question "Who can endure your words/anger?" (implying no one can) elevates her speech to a lethal force. The hyperbole "You fill the cup of anger, I drink it" (owQdHkjh ewdrk cqyk; vki cksfy gS) portrays the speaker willingly consuming her wrath, framing her anger as a sacred offering. Together, they characterize Latika as a sovereign whose every mood is absolute and the speaker as a devotee who accepts both nectar and poison. A wrong answer that treats the rhetorical question as a genuine inquiry ("Maybe someone else can endure it") fails to see the poetic convention of exaggeration for devotional effect.

questions.q: Compare the portrayal of Latika in Poem 1 (where she is addressed as the *recipient* of verses) with Poem 2 (where she is the *source* of anger/words the speaker endures). Analyze how the shift in grammatical agency (she receives vs. she acts) changes her character from a passive muse to an active divine power.
questions.a: In Poem 1, Latika is the grammatical object ("for Latika"), static and receptive; the poet *gives*. In Poem 2, she is the implied subject of "vukdkuh" (your words) and the agent of "owQdHkjh" (filling the cup); she *acts* and the poet *receives*. This shift transforms her from a dedicatee into an active deity who tests the devotee. A wrong answer that says "She is the same in both" ignores the structural reversal of agency that is central to the bhakti tradition's progression from offering to surrender.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Latika in Kukuan's poems is not a real woman but a literary symbol of the Divine Beloved." Defend your position using at least two specific textual strategies (e.g., lack of physical description, use of stock bhakti metaphors, absence of reciprocal dialogue).
questions.a: The claim is strongly supported. Strategy 1: Zero physical description — no eyes, hair, gait — only abstract effects (cooling heart, weighing body). Strategy 2: Stock bhakti metaphors (fire/water, cup of poison, testing devotee) align her with Krishna/Radha or God/devotee tropes, not individual portraiture. Strategy 3: She never speaks; the dialogue is monologic. A wrong answer that insists "She must be real because the poet says she lived in Delhi" confuses biographical context with textual construction; the *text* erases her individuality to elevate her to archetype.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza (in Hindi or Braj) that *Latika herself might speak* in reply to the poet, maintaining the same metaphorical register (fire/water, cup/gaze) but reversing the power dynamic. Explain your choice of one metaphor.
questions.a: Example stanza: "मेरा ताप तुम्हारी शीतलता, मेरा क्रोध तुम्हारा अमृत / तुम जो पीते हो विष सदा, मैं हूँ तुम्हारी ही छाया।" (My heat is your coolness, my anger your nectar / You who always drink poison, I am your own shadow.) The metaphor "I am your shadow" reverses the gaze: she exists only as his projection, yet claims ownership of the dynamic. A poor answer would write a modern, colloquial reply ("Okay, thanks for the poems") breaking the register and missing the analytical requirement to sustain the poem's symbolic logic.
